items.title: Dropping missiles from orbit? 2 European companies sign agreement to study the idea
items.summary:
A pair of companies in Europe have signed an agreement to study the feasibility of developing weapons that can be dropped from orbit. 

Atmos, a space company known for its Phoenix reusable reentry vehicle , will work with MBDA, Europe's largest missile manufacturer, on the new project. 

"We are assessing how proven defense systems and new orbital technologies can be combined to strengthen Europe's conventional deterrence and enable future defense capabilities," Sebastian Klaus, the CEO of Atmos Space Cargo, said in a statement on Nov. 18. 

The system that the companies are investigating is called Precision Orbital Deep Strike, or PODS. The companies said that their initial scope will center on design and feasibility, as well as technology integration. 

Atmos and MBDA also said this work could lead to demonstrations, but the companies' announcement makes it clear that any deployment or use would be subject to the approval of governmental and military authorities.

"The initiative also directly supports MBDA's broader strategic vision in the space domain, reinforcing both space for defense and the defense of space," Thomas Gottschild, MBDA Deutschland managing director, said in the same statement. 

This news comes a few months after Chief of Space Operations Gen. Douglas Schiess said that the U.S. Space Force operates orbital weapons .

"Let me be crystal clear: Today, Guardians operate on-orbit weapons that can defend the joint force against space-enabled attacks," Schiess said during a conferenace presentation on Sept. 15 ("Guardians" refers to Space Force personnel.)…
items.t: Dropping missiles from orbit? 2 European companies sign agreement to study the idea

items.title: Who turned the W upside down? Why Cassiopeia won't sit still
items.summary:
Some constellations are like old friends. You know them well, they're always there, and they never seem to change. A case in point is Cassiopeia, the queen. Its beautiful name comes from Greek mythology — the mother of Andromeda — and its shape is said to represent a queen sitting on a throne. To a stargazer, Cassiopeia is best known as a prominent northern constellation shaped like the letter W.

It's easy to find — look north, find five reasonably bright stars making a W, congratulate yourself on finding Cassiopeia and use it to get somewhere more interesting. It's so often a signpost, not a destination.

But look north a few hours after dark this month, and you'll notice the W has gone. The five stars are still there, but the shape you may have memorized looks like it's been picked up and turned over. It looks more like an E or an M, depending on when you look. Now try and look for the Big Dipper /the Plough. It's gone.

Nothing mysterious has happened, of course. Cassiopeia is doing exactly what it always does, but it's a reminder that the northern sky is where you can easily watch the stars move — and the seasons turn.

What's happening and when to look 

Stars move anti-clockwise around the north celestial pole, so Cassiopeia changes orientation. (Image credit: Alan Dyer/Stocktrek Images via Getty Images) Late November is an excellent time to reacquaint yourself with Cassiopeia from anywhere in the Northern Hemisphere. Look high in the northern sky during the evening for its five prominent stars — Caph, Schedar, Navi, Ruchbah and Segin. Depending on exactly when you…
items.t: Who turned the W upside down? Why Cassiopeia won't sit still

items.title: On this day in space! Nov. 27, 1885: Astronomer captures 1st known photo of a meteor during an Andromedid meteor storm
items.summary:
On Nov. 27, 1885, an astronomer made the first known photograph of a meteor. 

The picture was taken by Austro-Hungarian astronomer Ladislaus Weinek. He captured the trail of the meteor on a photographic plate in the Czech Republic. 

The meteor he captured was part of the Andromedid meteor shower . The Andromedids were associated with Biela's Comet , which broke apart in the 1850s. 

When Weinek observed the meteor shower in 1885, it was in the middle of a meteor storm . This means that there were way more meteors than usual. Skywatchers could see thousands of meteors per hour. 

The November 1872 incidence of the Andromedid meteor shower, as seen over France, in a painting. (Image credit: Alto Vintage Images/Alamy) Why it mattered Not many stargazers may be be acquainted with the Andromedid meteor shower. What used to be a spectacular annual meteor shower is now hardly even visible. 

But in 1885, the Andromedids were an annual treat for skywatchers hoping for a chance to see the remains of Biela's comet (a comet first spotted in 1772 and then found - for the third time - in 1826 by the German astronomer Wilhelm von Biela, from whom it gets its name). 

Meteor Shower Quiz: How Well Do You Know 'Shooting Stars'? 

This modern photo of the Geminid meteor shower shows dozens of meteors captured in a long exposure by Josh Drury. Ladislaus Weinek, who captured the first photo of a meteor, had to use a photographic plate in 1889. (Image credit: Josh Dury) Camera technology has come a long way since 1885, which is good since it is a bit harder to see the Andromedids these days.…
items.t: On this day in space! Nov. 27, 1885: Astronomer captures 1st known photo of a meteor during an Andromedid meteor storm

items.title: Astronomers watch a red giant star greedily devour a stellar 'Bao bun' before erupting: 'We couldn't quite believe our luck'
items.summary:
Astronomers witnessed the spectacular cosmic indigestion that resulted from a red giant star that devoured a stellar Bao bun in the form of its smaller companion star.

That isn't a random comparison. The cannibal star, which is 350 times bigger than the sun, is nicknamed "Big Bao," while its unfortunate companion had the nickname "Little Bao." The cute cosmic monikers come from the fact that this destructive merger event has been designated AT2025abao.

A Bao bun might be a little snack for a human, but this red giant star made a real meal out of Little Bao. This cannibalistic event was tracked by a wide array of ground- and space-based telescopes, including NASA space missions NEOWISE, SPHEREx, and the James Webb Space Telescope (JWST), as well as the W. M. Keck Observatory in Hawaii. The conclusion of the event AT2025abao was marked by a massive eruption witnessed in Oct. 2025 by two instruments at Caltech's Palomar Observatory: the Zwicky Transient Facility (ZTF) and the Wide-field INfrared Transient ExploreR (WINTER).

"The excitement was real," team member Viraj Karambelkar of Columbia University said in a statement sent to Space.com via email. "We couldn't quite believe our luck. With detailed observations for several years before the merger, for the first time, we now have an unprecedented glimpse of the conditions that lead to such cosmic events."

Reconstructing a violent cosmic collision The story of AT2025abao began when astronomers detected a bright flash in the nearby Andromeda galaxy , a region where scientists hadn't expected to see a cosmic explosion.…
items.t: Astronomers watch a red giant star greedily devour a stellar 'Bao bun' before erupting: 'We couldn't quite believe our luck'

The Moon Watchers 

Explanation: On November 24 , all denizens of our fair planet could watch the Moon rise opposite the setting Sun. Easy to spot in twilight skies above fields, fences, backyards, and even stone walls, the Moon was big and bright, and at its full phase . Known to some as a Beaver Moon, November’s Full Moon was also near perigee, the closest point in its elliptical orbit around planet Earth. That made it one of the biggest and brightest Full Moons, also known as a supermoon . In fact, November’s Full Moon was the first in a series of four consecutive Full Moons near perigee. In the same way that Shivelyuch (also called Shiveluch) frequently displays volcanic activity, it is also chronically obscured by clouds. When the OLI (Operational Land Imager) on Landsat 9  captured this image on November 8, 2026, clouds encroached on the snowy mountain on Russia’s Kamchatka Peninsula . But they hovered beneath the volcano’s 3,283-meter (10,771-foot) peak, leaving a clear opening over its caldera and northern upper slopes.

The upper reaches of Shivelyuch feature a caldera 9 kilometers (5.6 miles) wide that is open to the south. A lava dome , formed by vents extruding viscous magma, appears as a dark area within it. Lava domes on Shivelyuch go through cycles of growth and collapse, with collapses sometimes setting off fast-moving avalanches of hot ash and rock called pyroclastic flows .

items.title: 'Star Trek IV: The Voyage Home' at 40: 'Trek' has never been as joyous or fun as in 'the one with the whales'
items.summary:
It may have been subtitled "The Voyage Home", but to most viewers "Star Trek IV" (which has just turned 40) will always be "the one with the whales". 

After "The Wrath of Khan" and "The Search for Spock" went to some pretty dark places — ear worms, the destruction of the Enterprise, the death (and later resurrection) of a certain beloved Vulcan — the franchise was in need of some light relief. So what better than to set coordinates for the then-present day of 1986 San Francisco, for a time-travel comedy romp?

Spock himself, Leonard Nimoy, had directed "The Search for Spock" and Paramount had lined him up to call the shots on a follow-up before the movie had even landed in theaters. 

They gave him freedom to tell the story he wanted to tell, and he landed on a not obviously box-office-friendly formula of "No dying, no fighting, no shooting, no photon torpedoes, no phaser blasts, no stereotypical bad guy". It was a massive shift away from Khan and Kruge, the grandstanding villains in movies II and III. 

Nimoy also wanted the film to have an environmental message and appeal beyond the franchise's traditional fanbase. The film would actually be promoted with minimal "Trek" branding in some territories.

(Image credit: Paramount) "I wanted to make it accessible to people who don't go to 'Star Trek' movies," Nimoy said in "The Fifty-Year Mission" by Edward Gross and Mark A. Altman. "I wanted to make it a movie-movie. It starts out like a 'Star Trek' movie and then makes a left turn. It is intentionally very different."

"The Voyage Home" effectively closes the trilogy that…

As an inner planet, Venus never strays far from the horizon, at least compared to outer planets like Jupiter and Mars which can be visible all night long during opposition, when they shine opposite the sun in Earth's sky. 

Instead, Venus alternates between morning and evening appearances. All the while, its shifting moon-like phases and ever-changing proximity to Earth causes its brightness to wax and wane.

When is Venus at its most dazzling? Venus will reach peak brightness during its current morning apparition at 1:37 p.m. EST (1837 GMT) on Nov. 27 according to the astronomy website In-The-Sky . Stargazers in the U.S. could get an incredible view of Venus in the predawn hours of the coming week, as the planet climbs into the southeastern sky ahead of the rising sun, with Mercury clinging close to the horizon below.

items.title: On this day in space! Nov. 26, 2011: NASA's 2-ton nuclear-powered Curiosity rover launches to Mars
items.summary:
On November 26, 2011, the NASA Curiosity rover launched to Mars. 

The Mars rover Curiosity was the biggest and most powerful rover anyone had ever sent to the Red Planet. The 2-ton science laboratory is about the size of a small SUV. The mission's goal was to search for habitable environments on Mars , or evidence that the planet could have been habitable in the past. 

It launched on an Atlas V rocket from Cape Canaveral Air Force Station in Florida. About nine months later, Curiosity made a challenging landing on Mars. It successfully used a new landing technology called a sky crane to gently lower it to the surface. 

NASA's Curiosity rover lifts off atop a United Launch Alliance Atlas V rocket on Nov. 26, 2011 from Florida's Cape Canaveral Air Force Station. (Image credit: collectSPACE/Robert Z. Pearlman ) Why it mattered It may be hard to imagine now, but 15 years ago, the idea of a nuclear-powered rover on Mars was just a concept. When the Curiosity rover launched in 2011, it made that idea a reality the car-size probe (using a plutonium-based radioisotope thermoelectric generator that converts heat from radioactive decay into power) as it headed to the Red Planet. 

Curiosity was the largest rover ever launched to Mars, following up on the success of the tiny Sojourner rover in 1997 and the larger twin rovers Spirit and Opportunity in 2004. Its sky crane landing system was novel at the time, and fully automated. Once it began its descent in August 2012, NASA could only wait through "seven minutes of terror" to see how it turned out. It ended being a huge success.…
items.t: On this day in space! Nov. 26, 2011: NASA's 2-ton nuclear-powered Curiosity rover launches to Mars

An image captured by the Dark Energy Camera showcasing the Betta Fish Nebula. (Image credit: CTIO/NOIRLab/DOE/NSF/AURA) The striking blue of the Betta Fish Nebula swims across the cosmic landscape, a stunning wisp of material leftover from a stellar explosion. 

What is it? Roughly 6,800 light-years from Earth and nestled in the Centaurus constellation, this piece of the supernova remnant SNR G295.5+09.7 has earned the nickname the Betta Fish Nebula for its floaty, fishy shape. 

This almost ghostly whirl of gas and dust was created when a star much more massive than our sun exploded, blasting its outer layers of material outward in the process. Over time, the remnants of this supernova eruption stretched outward into space, dispersing and colliding with surrounding gas. The explosive remnants mixing with gas in the interstellar medium created this glowing, blue cloud.

This celestial scene was captured by the Dark Energy Camera (DECam), that was created by the U.S. Department of Energy. The camera is installed on the National Science Foundation's Víctor M. Blanco 4-meter Telescope in Chile. 

Why is it incredible? This image of a colossal, cosmic "fish" was captured by a camera meant to study the illusive effects of dark energy , which is the name scientists have given for whatever mysterious something is causing the universe to expand at an accelerating rate .

The camera is used as part of the Dark Energy Survey, a six-year, international collaboration in which scientists have collected observations of hundreds of millions of galaxies, thousands of supernova and…

items.title: Chang'e-6 Samples Reveal the Violent Chain Reaction That Built the Moon’s Largest Crater
items.summary: One of the most prominent features on the Moon is one we can’t regularly see, at least not completely. The South Pole-Aitken (SPA) basin is one of the largest, oldest, and deepest impact craters on the Moon, and until recently we’ve only been able to observe it from afar - and even then only when we sent orbiters around to the far side, which is never in direct line of sight with the Earth. Recently China has been busily sending landers and rovers to the site, and a new paper, published in Science Advances, details the actual samples returned to Earth by the Chang’e-6 mission and combines them with the in-situ data from the Chang’e-4 mission and rover. Those details combine to form a complete geological history of the major impacts that formed the basin, and some insight into the age of other impact craters scattered throughout the solar system.
items.t: Chang'e-6 Samples Reveal the Violent Chain Reaction That Built the Moon’s Largest Crater

And you'll get a big kick out of your Turkey Day guests uttering all the "oohs" and "ahs" or exclamations of "Wow!" with just one peek through the eyepiece. 

As darkness falls, Saturn will glow at first magnitude, shining with a sedate, yellow-white light and appearing noticeably brighter than the star Fomalhaut, about 40 degrees (the equivalent of four fist-widths) to its lower right.

The Milky Way shines bright in the sky of Brazil , over the white sand dunes and dark lagoons of Lençóis Maranhenses National Park . This composite image was taken later in the night in July from a latitude of approximately 2º south. It shows some prominent Milky Way features, such as dark dust lanes and colorful nebulas . items.title: December full moon 2026: When, where and how to see the Cold Moon
items.summary:
The December full moon reaches peak illumination at 8:28 p.m. EST on Dec. 23 (0128 GMT on Dec. 24) as the lunar disk shines opposite the sun in Earth's sky. It is often called the "Cold Moon" in reference to the frigid temperatures that prevail in the Northern Hemisphere around the time of its rising, according to the Old Farmer's Almanac . 

December's full moon will also occur close to perigee — the moon's closest point to Earth in its elliptical orbit — giving rise to a spectacular supermoon. A supermoon can appear 30% brighter and 14% larger than a full moon at its farthest point from Earth (also known as a micromoon).. 

According to the late, great astronomer Fred Espenak , the Cold Moon will be just 221,667 miles (356,740 kilometers) from Earth when it turns full, making it the closest supermoon of 2026!

When to see the December full moon The full Cold Supermoon will make for a spectacular sight when it rises over the eastern horizon at sunset on Dec. 23, mere hours before reaching maximum illumination. Remember to use Time and Date's moonrise and moonset tracker for timings specific to your location. 

Earth's satellite may appear larger than normal while close to the horizon. This is partly because it is near perigee, when it appears subtly larger in the night sky, but also because of a phenomenon called the moon illusion, which tricks us into perceiving the moon to be bigger than it actually is while in the presence of foreground objects.

items.title: NASA Eyes Crop Candidates for Future Menus
items.summary:
As NASA prepares for future missions to the Moon and Mars, researchers are studying crops that could provide astronauts with fresh food, nutrition, and variety far from Earth. Such crop variety can help with menus in deep space, something top of mind this week as the nation celebrates Thanksgiving.   

Strawberries (left) grown in the Space Life Sciences Lab’s controlled environment chamber. Cucumbers (center) and lemon basil (right) grown in a controlled environment chamber at NASA’s Kennedy Space Center in Florida. 
 NASA 

Recent testing points to strawberries, cucumbers, and lemon basil as potential options for future explorers. Space crops can absorb carbon dioxide, produce oxygen, and recycle water. These capabilities will become increasingly important as crewed missions extend farther from our home planet.

While space crop research advances on Earth, capabilities are also expanding in space. A new investigation from NASA’s Biological and Physical Sciences Division is set to launch to the International Space Station, where the first-of-its-kind prototype growth chamber will provide critical insights for developing crop production systems that could grow crops like these for future Moon Base habitats and Mars missions.

Sweet space strawberries 
 Strawberries are among the few sweet fruits under consideration for spaceflight and are nutritious, aromatic, and self-pollinating.

Researchers at NASA’s Kennedy Space Center in Florida are growing strawberries in flight-like growth chambers to evaluate the potential space crop, and NASA partners at The Australian Research…
items.t: NASA Eyes Crop Candidates for Future Menus

items.title: ALMA Reveals a Dying Star's Final Breath, Encoded In a Giant Ring of Gas
items.summary: About 6,500 years ago, a dying star emitted its final thermal pulse. That dying breath created a giant ring of gas detected by ALMA. Then only 700 years ago, the star formed an hourglass nebula. Theory predicted this, but this is the first direct evidence supporting it.
items.t: ALMA Reveals a Dying Star's Final Breath, Encoded In a Giant Ring of Gas

items.title: Childhood, Career Come Full Circle for Budget Analyst at NASA Goddard
items.summary:
Conversations about NASA were the norm around the dinner table during Ashley Knight’s childhood. Her parents worked at NASA’s Goddard Space Flight Center in Greenbelt, Maryland, and discussions about happenings at the agency continued even when they came home from the office.

“I remember a poignant dialogue we had after the space shuttle Challenger disaster,” Knight recalled. “However, we talked just as much about the engaging work my parents were doing inside Goddard’s gates.”

Her father Lyle Knight was a mechanical engineer, while her mother Julia Knight worked the bulk of her career in human resources. They brought their daughter on center for Take Your Child to Work Day and other events, and over time she became hooked.

“I saw the chambers where spacecraft and instruments were being tested, as well as other facilities used to help further space exploration. Above all, I witnessed the passion and collaborative spirit everyone had at Goddard,” Knight said. “As a child, I found it incredibly fascinating.”

Ashley Knight (right) on a visit to NASA’s Goddard Space Flight Center in Greenbelt, Md., while her parents were employees. Photo courtesy of Ashley Knight 

It all came full circle in late August when, after growing up around NASA and later working several contractor roles for the agency, Knight and a number of her colleagues in the Goddard Office of the Chief Financial Officer were sworn in as federal employees as part of a workforce directive to strengthen the agency’s technical core competencies by bringing mission-critical positions into the civil service.

She…
items.t: Childhood, Career Come Full Circle for Budget Analyst at NASA Goddard

items.title: Eye of the Sahara
items.summary:
NASA/Luke Delaney 

The Richat Structure, also known as the “Eye of the Sahara,” is seen from the International Space Station as it orbited above on Nov. 14, 2026. It is an eroded geological dome about 100 million years old created by igneous activity and uplift in the nation of Mauritania. In this type of geologic structure, rocks exposed in the center of the “bullseye” are older than rocks forming the outer rings. This structure measures 45 kilometers (28 miles) across and is made up of igneous and sedimentary rocks.

Image credit: NASA/Luke Delaney
items.t: Eye of the Sahara

items.title: Using Lunar Craters as Free Radiation Shields for Moon Base Nuclear Reactors
items.summary: Powering any future lunar base is a massive engineering challenge. The two-week lunar night can drain batteries charged by solar panels during the two-week day, if the batteries themselves can even withstand the freezing temperatures that go along with it. So, for decades at this point, engineers have planned to use a nuclear reactor to at least partially power any future human settlement on the Moon. A new paper from researchers at Los Alamos, NASA Glenn, Oak Ridge, Idaho National Lab, and Lockheed Martin, and presented at the American Nuclear Society’s Nuclear and Emerging Technologies for Space (NETS) conference back in April, offers a simple solution to one major problem for any such future nuclear reactor - shielding.
items.t: Using Lunar Craters as Free Radiation Shields for Moon Base Nuclear Reactors

items.title: A New Discovery is Re-Drawing the Map of the Milky Way
items.summary: New research shows that star formation is occurring in the Milky Way's central bar. This goes against previous research, and against observations of other barred spiral galaxies. The discovery by a PhD student shows a vast rotating structure of stars near the centre of our Galaxy is driving enormous shock fronts through clouds of gas, compressing them and creating conditions for new stars to form.
items.t: A New Discovery is Re-Drawing the Map of the Milky Way

items.title: Comet Encke's Shape and Heat Revealed in Thermal Glow
items.summary: Comets are time capsules of the origins of the solar system, containing materials that have existed for billions of years. While comets primarily orbit in the farthest reaches of the solar system, specifically the Kuiper Belt or Oort Cloud, some make their way closer to the Sun. When this happens, the increased heat cause cometary icy material to evaporate, producing a spectacular tail while also revealing the rocky material underneath, known as a comet’s nucleus. But how well can astronomers use telescopic observations to study the composition and temperatures of a cometary nucleus?
items.t: Comet Encke's Shape and Heat Revealed in Thermal Glow

items.title: Maybe Dark Energy Isn't so Inexplicable After All
items.summary: The Universe as we know it is comprised of three "things": baryonic matter (planets, stars, galaxies, us), dark matter (still unexplained) and dark energy (really, really still unexplained). Of the three, dark energy remains challenging because it's driving the acceleration of the expanding Universe. However, we can't see it, or even put a description to it, other than, "it's mysterious".
items.t: Maybe Dark Energy Isn't so Inexplicable After All

items.title: A Brief-ish History of METI. Part IV: Millennial METI Experiments
items.summary: We continue with the history of METI with a look at public attempts to send messages to the cosmos around the turn of the century.
items.t: A Brief-ish History of METI. Part IV: Millennial METI Experiments

items.title: A Gigantic Stellar Eruption Spreads Planetary Material Into Space
items.summary: Asymptotic Giant Branch (AGB) stars spread heavy elements into space with their stellar winds. This material eventually forms more stars, and even rocky planets like ours. For a long time, astronomers thought this important mass-loss was driven by stellar winds. But new research shows how magnetic fields play an important role. A vast flare and magnetic loop of material from the AGB star Mira provides the evidence.
items.t: A Gigantic Stellar Eruption Spreads Planetary Material Into Space

items.title: The Rise of Astrosociology: What Can Analogue Astronaut Studies Teach us About the Future of Humanity in Space?
items.summary: The Astrosociology Research Institute was founded in 2008 as part of a growing movement dedicated to examining humanity's future in space through the lens of the social sciences and related disciplines. The goal is to approach human spaceflight with the intent of ensuring that humanity will not only survive in space, but flourish.
items.t: The Rise of Astrosociology: What Can Analogue Astronaut Studies Teach us About the Future of Humanity in Space?
